title: Piaget and Cognitive Stages
description: How children build knowledge — schemas, assimilation, and the four stages

concepts.title: Schemas, Assimilation, and Accommodation
concepts.contentHtml:
Jean Piaget (1896–1980) treated children not as miniature adults but as active constructors of knowledge. His central unit was the schema — an organised pattern of thought or action used to make sense of experience.

Schemas develop through two complementary processes:

Assimilation: incorporating new information into an existing schema. A child who calls every four-legged animal 'dog' is assimilating cats and horses to the dog schema.
Accommodation: revising the schema when assimilation fails. Eventually the child accommodates by splitting the schema into 'dog,' 'cat,' and 'horse.'

Cognitive growth is driven by equilibration — the drive to resolve disequilibrium between schema and reality. Piaget's epistemology was constructivist: knowledge is built through interaction with the world, not transmitted ready-made from adults.

concepts.title: The Four Stages
concepts.contentHtml:
Piaget proposed four universal, sequential stages of cognitive development:

Sensorimotor (0–2): infants know the world through action and sensation. The major achievement is object permanence — understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight, typically around 8 months.

Preoperational (2–7): symbolic thought emerges, but reasoning is egocentric (the child cannot easily take another's viewpoint) and lacks conservation — the understanding that quantity is preserved despite changes in appearance.

Concrete operational (7–11): children master conservation, classification, and reversibility, but only for tangible problems.

Formal operational (11+): adolescents reason hypothetically and abstractly, handling propositions detached from concrete instances.

concepts.title: Critiques and Revisions
concepts.contentHtml:
Piaget's stage theory has been hugely influential but is no longer accepted in its strict form.

He underestimated infants. Renée Baillargeon's violation-of-expectation studies in the 1980s showed infants as young as 3.5 months display surprise when objects appear to violate physical laws — suggesting object permanence is present far earlier than Piaget claimed.

Stages are less discrete than proposed. Children show 'horizontal décalage' — mastering conservation of number before volume, for instance. Development is more domain-specific than Piaget allowed.

Cultural context matters. Formal operational thought is not universal; it depends on schooling and is sensitive to task content.

Modern neo-Piagetian theorists (Case, Karmiloff-Smith) preserve constructivism while abandoning rigid stages.

title: Vygotsky and Sociocultural Development
description: Mind built through culture, language, and the zone of proximal development

concepts.title: The Sociocultural Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Lev Vygotsky (1896–1934) offered a radical alternative to Piaget. Where Piaget saw the child as a lone scientist, Vygotsky saw cognition as socially constructed. Higher mental functions originate in social interaction and are only later internalised by the individual.

His general genetic law of cultural development: every function appears twice — first between people (interpsychological), then within the child (intrapsychological).

Culture provides psychological tools — language, number systems, writing, mnemonic devices — that mediate and reshape thinking. A child counting on fingers is not just using a body part but a culturally inherited system. Without these tools, distinctively human cognition does not develop.

Vygotsky's work, suppressed under Stalin, was rediscovered in the West in the 1960s and now rivals Piaget's in influence.

concepts.title: The Zone of Proximal Development
concepts.contentHtml:
Vygotsky's most cited concept is the zone of proximal development (ZPD): the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can achieve with guidance from a more capable partner.

What lies in the ZPD today will become the child's independent ability tomorrow. Instruction should target this zone — too easy is wasted, too hard is fruitless.

The American psychologists Wood, Bruner, and Ross (1976) coined scaffolding to describe the temporary support an adult provides: prompting, modelling, simplifying, then gradually withdrawing as competence grows. Effective teaching is calibrated, contingent assistance.

The ZPD reframes assessment too: a child's potential is better measured by what they can do with help than by static IQ-style tests, which only capture independent performance.

concepts.title: Language and Thought
concepts.contentHtml:
Vygotsky and Piaget famously disagreed about private speech — children talking to themselves while playing or working. Piaget viewed it as egocentric, a sign of cognitive immaturity that fades.

Vygotsky argued the opposite: private speech is the internalisation of social dialogue. Children first regulate their behaviour using speech with others; this becomes self-directed speech aloud, then quiet muttering, then silent inner speech — the medium of adult verbal thought.

Empirical work has largely vindicated Vygotsky. Children use private speech more on difficult tasks and when correcting errors, and it predicts later self-regulation. Inner speech is now a serious topic in cognitive science (Charles Fernyhough), implicated in working memory, planning, and consciousness.

For Vygotsky, then, language doesn't just express thought — it constitutes a major part of it.

title: Attachment and Early Relationships
description: Bowlby, Harlow, and Ainsworth on the bonds that shape development

concepts.title: Bowlby's Attachment Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
John Bowlby (1907–1990) proposed that infants are biologically prepared to form a strong, selective bond with a primary caregiver. Drawing on ethology — particularly Konrad Lorenz's work on imprinting — he argued attachment is an evolved behavioural system that increases survival by keeping vulnerable infants close to protective adults.

The system is activated by threat, illness, or separation, and terminated by proximity and contact. From repeated interactions, the child builds an internal working model — a mental representation of self, caregiver, and relationships generally.

Bowlby's Attachment and Loss trilogy (1969–1980) reframed earlier psychoanalytic ideas. Attachment is not, as Freud thought, secondary to feeding (the 'cupboard love' theory), but a primary need in its own right. Love is not a by-product of nutrition.

concepts.title: Harlow's Monkeys
concepts.contentHtml:
Harry Harlow's experiments at the University of Wisconsin in the late 1950s decisively refuted the cupboard-love theory.

Infant rhesus monkeys were separated from their mothers and offered two surrogates: a wire mother dispensing milk and a cloth mother providing only soft contact. The infants drank from the wire mother but spent the vast majority of their time clinging to the cloth mother — and ran to her when frightened.

Harlow concluded that contact comfort, not feeding, is the foundation of attachment. Monkeys raised in isolation showed severe, often permanent social and emotional disturbance, demonstrating that early relationships are not optional add-ons but constitutive of normal development.

Today the studies are ethically troubling, but their findings transformed thinking about institutional childcare, hospital visiting policies, and orphanage practice.

concepts.title: Ainsworth and the Strange Situation
concepts.contentHtml:
Mary Ainsworth, Bowlby's collaborator, devised the Strange Situation (1969–1978) — a 20-minute laboratory procedure with eight episodes involving separations and reunions between a 12–18-month-old and caregiver, with a stranger present.

From the infant's reunion behaviour, Ainsworth identified three patterns:

Secure (~65%): distressed by separation, comforted by reunion, uses caregiver as a secure base.
Insecure–avoidant (~20%): shows little distress and avoids the caregiver on return.
Insecure–resistant/ambivalent (~10–15%): highly distressed and difficult to soothe, simultaneously seeking and resisting contact.

Mary Main later added disorganised attachment — incoherent, contradictory behaviour often linked to frightening or unpredictable caregiving.

Attachment classifications show modest stability into adulthood and predict later social competence, but they are not destiny: relationships and reflective work can revise the working model.

title: Identity, Morality, and Adolescence
description: Erikson, Kohlberg, Marcia, and the storms of becoming

concepts.title: Erikson's Psychosocial Stages
concepts.contentHtml:
Erik Erikson (1902–1994) extended Freud's developmental thinking across the entire lifespan. He proposed eight psychosocial stages, each defined by a central conflict that must be resolved well enough to support the next.

The early stages — trust vs. mistrust, autonomy vs. shame, initiative vs. guilt, industry vs. inferiority — cover infancy through middle childhood. Adolescence brings identity vs. role confusion: forming a coherent sense of self that integrates values, abilities, and social roles.

Adulthood continues the work: intimacy vs. isolation (young adulthood), generativity vs. stagnation (caring for the next generation in middle age), and ego integrity vs. despair (accepting one's life as meaningful in old age).

Erikson's framework remains influential for treating development as a lifelong negotiation, not a process completed in childhood.

concepts.title: Marcia's Identity Statuses
concepts.contentHtml:
James Marcia (1966) operationalised Erikson's identity stage by crossing two dimensions: exploration (active questioning of values, careers, identities) and commitment (settling on choices).

This yields four identity statuses:

Identity diffusion: no exploration, no commitment — drift.
Foreclosure: commitment without exploration — values adopted wholesale from parents or community.
Moratorium: active exploration without commitment — the classic adolescent crisis.
Identity achievement: commitment after genuine exploration.

Marcia's typology is not a fixed sequence — adults can revisit moratorium during crises. Cross-cultural research shows the statuses vary in prevalence: foreclosure is more common in traditional collectivist contexts, moratorium more common where prolonged adolescence and choice are culturally encouraged. The framework remains a workhorse of identity research.

concepts.title: Kohlberg's Moral Stages and Their Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
Lawrence Kohlberg (1927–1987) used moral dilemmas — most famously the Heinz dilemma, in which a man considers stealing a drug to save his wife — to map the reasoning behind moral judgments, not the verdicts themselves.

He proposed three levels with two stages each:

Preconventional: avoid punishment; pursue rewards.
Conventional: maintain relationships and social order.
Postconventional: reason from social-contract principles and universal ethical principles.

Carol Gilligan (In a Different Voice, 1982) argued Kohlberg's scheme privileged abstract justice reasoning typical of his male samples and undervalued an ethic of care and responsiveness more often found in his female subjects.

Jonathan Haidt's later social intuitionist model went further: most moral judgment is fast intuition; conscious reasoning is largely post-hoc justification. Stage theories may overestimate the role of deliberate reasoning in everyday morality.

title: Language, Adulthood, and Aging
description: Critical periods, lifelong development, and the cognitively aging mind

concepts.title: Language Acquisition and Critical Periods
concepts.contentHtml:
Noam Chomsky argued in the late 1950s that children acquire language too rapidly, and from too sparse and noisy input, to be learning it by general-purpose induction. He proposed an innate Language Acquisition Device (LAD) — a domain-specific cognitive system encoding the abstract structure (Universal Grammar) common to all human languages. This was a frontal assault on B.F. Skinner's behaviourist account of language as verbal habit.

Eric Lenneberg (1967) added the critical period hypothesis: full native-like mastery requires exposure before puberty. Evidence comes from rare cases like Genie, the girl isolated until age 13, who never acquired normal grammar despite intensive teaching, and from second-language learners who plateau short of native fluency.

Modern usage-based theorists (Tomasello) push back, emphasising that infants are powerful statistical learners and social interpreters — language need not require a dedicated module.

concepts.title: Emerging and Adult Development
concepts.contentHtml:
Jeffrey Arnett (2000) named a new life stage: emerging adulthood (roughly 18–25 in industrialised societies). It is characterised by identity exploration, instability, self-focus, feeling 'in-between,' and a sense of possibility. Arnett argued it is not delayed adolescence but a distinct period created by extended education and later marriage.

In middle adulthood, Erikson's generativity vs. stagnation describes the central task: contributing to the next generation through parenting, mentoring, or creative work. Generativity predicts well-being and is a stronger correlate of midlife meaning than income or status.

Late adulthood is governed in Erikson's scheme by ego integrity vs. despair: looking back on one's life and finding it coherent and acceptable, or being overwhelmed by regret. Robert Butler's life review describes the spontaneous reminiscing through which older adults integrate their stories.

concepts.title: Cognitive Aging and Socioemotional Selectivity
concepts.contentHtml:
Aging affects different cognitive abilities differently. Raymond Cattell's distinction is central: fluid intelligence (reasoning with novel material, processing speed, working memory) declines steadily from the 20s. Crystallised intelligence (vocabulary, accumulated knowledge, expertise) is preserved or grows into the 70s.

Paul Baltes's selective optimisation with compensation describes how older adults maintain function: selecting fewer goals, optimising remaining capacities by practice, and compensating with strategies and tools. The pianist Arthur Rubinstein played fewer pieces, practised them more, and slowed before fast passages so they sounded faster by contrast.

Laura Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory shows that as people perceive time as limited, they prioritise emotional meaning over information-seeking — pruning social networks to close ties and reporting greater well-being. Aging is loss and reorganisation, not simple decline.
